n: The bride humbly calls herself a common wildflower of the Sharon plain and the valleys. Many Christians later applied the phrase “rose of Sharon” to Christ, though here the bride speaks of herself.

f.g: Probably a crocus or similar wildflower of the coastal plain of Sharon.

n: The groom answers: compared to other young women, she is like a lily surrounded by thorns.
She replies that compared to other young men, he is like a fruit tree in a forest — offering shade and sweet fruit.

f.g: Possibly the apricot or apple tree.
Shade was precious in a hot land — a picture of protection and rest.

n: He brought her to the banquet hall, and his love was displayed over her like a banner — openly and proudly.

f.g: A flag or standard showing whom one belongs to.

n: She asks to be refreshed with raisin cakes and fruit, because she is faint with love.
She describes his tender embrace and how secure she feels in his arms.
A refrain repeated in the book: she urges the young women not to awaken love before its proper time. Love should not be rushed.

f.r: Song of Solomon 3:5; Song of Solomon 8:4

n: She hears his voice! He comes bounding over the mountains and hills, eager to see her.
He is like a swift gazelle or young stag. Now he stands outside her wall, peering through the window lattice.

f.g: A wooden screen over a window.

n: He calls her to get up and come away with him.
Winter is over and the rainy season has ended. In Israel, the rains fall from about October to April.
Flowers bloom, birds sing, and the cooing of the turtledove is heard. Spring is a picture of love coming to life.

f.g: Turtledove, a migrating bird that arrives in spring.

n: The first figs ripen and the blossoming vines give off fragrance. Again he invites her to come away with him.

f.g: The early, unripe figs that appear in spring.

n: He calls her his dove hidden in the rock clefts and cliff ledges, longing to see her face and hear her voice.
Catch the little foxes that ruin the vineyards in bloom. Small problems, left alone, can damage a young and tender love.

f.g: Small pests that dig and gnaw at vines — a picture of small threats to love.

n: She declares their mutual commitment: he belongs to her and she to him. He pastures his flock among the lilies.

f.w: My beloved is mine, and I am his
f.r: Song of Solomon 6:3; Song of Solomon 7:10

n: She asks him to return quickly, like a gazelle on the rugged mountains, until morning breaks and the shadows flee.

f.g: Possibly “separation” or “cleft” — rugged, divided hills; the location is uncertain.
